scenes.heading: Structured Logging
scenes.narration: Production logs are read by machines, not humans. Let's move from fragile free-form strings to typed, queryable structured logging.

scenes.heading: Why structured beats fmt.Println
items: Free-form strings force fragile regex parsing downstream
Fields drift between call sites and can't be filtered
Typed key/value attributes are indexed and queryable
scenes.narration: A line like printf user-percent-s failed with err is cheap to write but expensive to operate. Your log backend must regex-parse it, fields drift between call sites, and you cannot filter level-equals-error and user-id-equals-forty-two. Structured logging emits typed key/value attributes, usually as JSON, so every field is indexed and queryable. Think of a log line as a row in a table, not a sentence in a diary.

scenes.heading: How slog is built
steps: A Logger is the front end you call
A Handler formats and writes — Text or JSON
Levels filter by a configurable minimum
With returns a child logger carrying attrs
scenes.narration: The standard log-slog splits the front end from the back end. A Logger is what you call; a Handler formats and writes, and the stdlib ships a Text handler for humans and a JSON handler for machines. Attributes attach typed data, a level gate filters by a configurable minimum, and With returns a child logger that stamps its attributes onto every subsequent line.

scenes.heading: One request ID on every line
scenes.narration: Here's the idiomatic pattern. Middleware mints a request ID, builds a child logger with With that carries the request-id and path, and stores it in the context. Then every handler down the chain logs through that context-scoped logger, so the same request-id appears automatically on every line the request produces — without passing a logger into every function.

scenes.text: zap and zerolog avoid slog's any-boxing for near-zero-allocation logging at high volume.
scenes.narration: For very high log volumes, slog's loose API boxes values into any, which allocates. Uber's zap takes strongly typed fields on an essentially zero-allocation core, and zerolog uses a chained fluent builder that writes JSON straight into a byte buffer. Both give you the same structured discipline with dramatically lower per-line cost.

scenes.text: Start with stdlib slog; reach for zap/zerolog only when profiling shows logging allocations matter.
scenes.narration: So start with the standard slog: it's fast, dependency-free, and more than enough for most services. Reserve Error for what a human should actually look at, use levels and sampling to control cost, and only reach for zap or zerolog when profiling proves logging allocations truly matter.
